searchNote: WebSearch worked this time. Each flagged item and every title/author/year pair was searched (encyclopedias, library catalogues, publisher and bookseller records). Where sources disagreed the text was softened or the disagreement stated. Several search summaries covered only part of a multi-item query; those items were re-searched singly or rest on solid recall and are listed under remainingDoubts.

corrected.was: A book's date can lag its journey by years or centuries: Bashō travelled in 1689 and the book appeared in 1702, and Montagu's letters were published after her death.
corrected.now: A book's date can lag its journey by years or decades: Bashō travelled in 1689 and the book appeared in 1702, and Montagu's letters of 1716 to 1718 were revised later and published in 1763, after her death.
corrected.why: Neither example is a lag of centuries (13 and 45 years). Sources also say Montagu revised the letters during her life, so 'written 1716 to 1718' alone overstated it.

corrected.was: made by young men of the European elite, roughly from the seventeenth to the early nineteenth century.
corrected.now: made by young men of the European elite, above all British, from the seventeenth century until railways and steamships opened travel to far more people.
corrected.why: Sources put the end at the railway era (from the 1840s, some say the 1870s), not the early nineteenth century; they also tie the Tour mainly to British nobility.

travel-writing.js.confirmed_notes: Confirmed by search: Bird 1879 (John Murray); Kingsley 1897; Montagu written 1716-1718, published 1763 (posthumous, unauthorised); Cook 1841 (text already says only that he began arranging excursions; 'first' is disputed so it is not claimed); Xuanzang's record completed 646 (seventh century); Marco Polo book written 1298-1299 (text says around 1300); Ibn Battuta's rihla dictated to Ibn Juzayy, finished 1355 or 1356 (text says 1350s); Bashō journey 1689, book 1702 posthumous; Sterne 1768; Twain 1869; Stevenson 1879; Lawrence Sea and Sardinia 1921 (New York, Seltzer; UK edition 1923); Fleming 1933; Greene 1936; Byron 1937; Stark 1934; Priestley 1934; West 1941; Durrell 1957; Newby 1958; Thesiger 1959; Steinbeck 1962; Naipaul 1964; Theroux 1975; Chatwin 1977; Leigh Fermor 1977; Matthiessen 1978; Said 1978; Davidson 1980; Fussell 1980; Raban 1981 (Collins); Heat-Moon 1982; Dalrymple 1989; Pratt 1992 (contact zone from her work); Bryson 1995; Cambridge Companion 2002; Stewart 2004 (UK).
remainingDoubts: Kinglake's Eothen 1844: confirmed as 1844 by search, though the journey was 1834-35; the text does not claim the journey date.
Dates for Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta are deliberately approximate; sources differ by a year or two.
The revival 'often placed in the mid-1970s and 1980s' is a loose dating and the facet is already set to contested.
The 70,000 to 100,000 word range is a general trade rule of thumb, worded as 'often given for narrative nonfiction' and consistent with the installed memoir and narrative-nonfiction profiles.

corrected.was: John Ruskin's term for attributing human feelings to nature, a habit nature writers are advised to watch.
corrected.now: John Ruskin's 1856 term for the false impressions strong feeling gives of nature, now mostly used for attributing human feelings to nature, a habit nature writers are advised to watch.
corrected.why: Ruskin (Modern Painters vol. 3, 1856) meant the falseness of perception under strong emotion; the 'attributing human feelings' sense is the later, looser usage.

corrected.was: gave it a legal meaning of land where people are visitors
corrected.now: gave it a legal meaning for protected federal land where people are visitors
corrected.why: The Act's definition (section 2(c)) applies to designated federal land and says man is a visitor who does not remain.

nature-writing.js.confirmed_notes: Confirmed by search: Pliny's Natural History (AD 77, first ten books; completed posthumously); Kamo no Chomei Hojoki 1212; Walden 1854 (two years, two months, two days at the pond, compressed into one year); Burroughs Wake-Robin 1871; Muir 1894; Austin 1903 (Houghton Mifflin); Beston 1928; Leopold 1949 (posthumous, land ethic); Carson 1951 and 1962; Baker 1967; Abbey 1968; Mabey 1973 (Collins); Dillard 1974; Lopez 1986; Williams 1991 (Pantheon); Shepherd written 1940s, published 1977; Deakin 1999; Jamie 2005; Macfarlane 2007; Macdonald 2014; Kimmerer 2013; Norton Book of Nature Writing (Finch and Elder, 1990); solastalgia coined by the Australian philosopher Glenn Albrecht (2003, published 2005); pathetic fallacy coined by Ruskin 1856; Wilderness Act 1964 wording; phenology (term coined 1849) and edgelands (named by Marion Shoard, popularised by Farley and Roberts 2011); the 'new nature writing' label was given wide currency by Granta 102 in 2008.
remainingDoubts: Selborne: bibliographic practice is 1789; whether it first appeared in December 1788 is reported by one source and not by others, so the text no longer commits to a publication year.
'New nature writing': no source found for who first used the phrase; the profile says only that it is a label used since the 2000s and disputed, which Granta 102 (2008) supports.
The profile's 'from about the turn of the millennium' for the British strand is approximate (Waterlog 1999, Findings 2005, The Wild Places 2007).

self-help.js.confirmed_notes: Confirmed by search: Smiles Self-Help 1859 (John Murray; the book popularised the phrase, sources do not support saying he coined it, and the text says only 'popularised'); Castiglione 1528; Franklin's almanac from 1732; Wattles 1910 (New Thought); Hill 1937 (listed among New Thought authors in a bibliography; text says 'often placed in its line'); New Thought rooted in the nineteenth century (Quimby); Carnegie 1936; Peale 1952; AA Big Book 1939; Beattie 1986; Maltz 1960; Peck 1978; Burns 1980 (Morrow); Jeffers 1987 (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich); Covey 1989; Chicken Soup for the Soul 1993; Johnson 1998; Byrne 2006; Ehrenreich 2009; Allen 2001 (Viking); Gray 1992 (HarperCollins); Tolle 1997 (Namaste Publishing, Vancouver; US edition 1999; agrees with the library); Cameron 1992; Pressfield 2002; Clear 2018; Dweck's Mindset 2006 with the effect-size debate; Maslow's self-actualisation; bibliotherapy defined as reading used to help with personal problems.
remainingDoubts: Hill and New Thought is a classification: bibliographies list him among New Thought authors, but not every scholar does; the text is hedged with 'often placed in its line'.
Origin of 'toxic positivity' was not found and is not claimed; the text calls it only 'a critics' term'.
Smiles may not have originated the phrase self-help; the text says he popularised it.
Length ranges (40,000 to 80,000 words) are author-services rules of thumb, not industry data; the facet is set to varies with asOf.
